meters.label: Route length as a percent of the optimum

frames.narration: A dispatcher must plan one round trip through 10 stops, as short as possible. Four ways to get an answer: try every order, search with pruning, or two quick heuristics.
Exhaustive search checks all 362,880 orders of the other 9 stops, in 986,409 steps, and proves that the shortest route has length 326. At this size exact is cheap: nothing to apologise for.

Branch and bound runs the same search but drops a partial route as soon as it is as long as the best known complete one. Same optimum of 326, in 131,060 steps. The worst case is unchanged; typical instances get much easier.

Now grow the problem. Tours number (n-1)!/2: 181,440 for 10 stops, 60,822,550,204,416,000 for 20, and 310,224,200,866,619,719,680,000 for 25. At a billion tours per second that is almost two years for 20 stops and 9,837,144 years for 25. This growth is what NP-hard warns about.

Nearest neighbour always drives to the closest unvisited stop: 45 steps, almost free. The route has length 456, which is 139% of the optimum. Fast, and 39% too long on this instance; other instances differ.

A 2-opt pass then reverses any stretch of the route whose reversal makes it shorter: 5 moves and 108 steps, and it reaches 326, the optimum. That is luck of a tiny instance. 2-opt only guarantees a route it cannot shorten by one reversal, a local optimum.

Dynamic programming over subsets avoids the factorial: about n squared times 2 to the n steps. For 30 stops that is 966,367,641,600 steps, about 16 minutes. But it stores 32,212,254,720 values, roughly 258 GB at 8 bytes each. Exponential growth hits memory before time.

What to do: ask for the real n and the real deadline. Small n: solve exactly. Larger: use a solver library if one exists, otherwise a heuristic plus local search, measured against a lower bound or small exact cases. An approximation algorithm gives a proven guarantee, such as 1.5 times the optimum for triangle-inequality tours.
